unit.title: TypeScript in practice
unit.description: Type annotations, interfaces and type aliases, unions and narrowing, optional fields, any versus unknown, generics, strict mode, tsconfig, the TypeScript 7 compiler

cards.definition: JavaScript with types added. The compiler checks the code before it runs and then removes the types: the browser or Node runs plain JavaScript. Errors show up in the editor instead of in production.
cards.example: function total(price: number, qty: number): number catches total("10", 2) before anyone runs it.

cards.definition: Two ways to name the shape of an object. interface Lead { email: string } and type Lead = { email: string } are close; type can also name unions such as type Status = "new" | "won" | "lost".
cards.example: type Channel = "seo" | "ads" | "email" refuses any other string.

cards.definition: A union says a value can be one of several types (string | number). Before using it, the code narrows it with a check such as typeof, in or a comparison, and TypeScript follows that check.
cards.example: if (typeof id === "string") { id.toUpperCase() } compiles; without the if, it does not.

cards.definition: A question mark marks a property that may be missing: phone?: string. Its type becomes string | undefined, so the code must handle the missing case.
any switches type checking off for a value: anything goes, bugs included. unknown also accepts any value but forces a check before use. Prefer unknown for data coming from outside (JSON, APIs).
cards.example: const data: unknown = await res.json(); then check it before reading data.email.

cards.definition: Type parameters that let a function or type work with many types while keeping them linked: function first<T>(items: T[]): T returns a string for a string array and a Lead for a Lead array.
cards.example: type ApiResponse<T> = { data: T; error?: string }

cards.definition: tsconfig.json configures the compiler. "strict": true turns on the checks that matter, such as null checks and no implicit any. New projects should always start strict.
cards.example: With strict on, let name: string = null is an error.

cards.definition: The compiler of TypeScript 7, released in July 2026: rewritten in Go, with builds and editor checks around ten times faster on large projects. The language itself stays the same.
cards.example: A monorepo that took 60 seconds to type-check now takes about 6.

exercises.prompt: What happens to TypeScript types when the code runs in the browser?
choices: They are removed: the browser runs plain JavaScript
The browser checks them on every function call
They slow the page down by 30 percent
They are converted into HTML attributes
exercises.explain: Types exist only at compile time. That is why data from an API still needs a runtime check.

exercises.prompt: Which line does the compiler reject?
exercises.explain: A string cannot go into a number variable. JavaScript would accept it silently and break later.

exercises.prompt: Which value is accepted by this type?
exercises.explain: A union of literal strings accepts exactly those values, case included. It is a cheap way to avoid typos in channel names.

exercises.prompt: Why does the compiler complain about the second line?
choices: id may be a number, and numbers have no toUpperCase
toUpperCase does not exist in TypeScript
Unions are forbidden in function parameters
The function must return a string type
exercises.explain: With a union, you narrow first: if (typeof id === "string") { ... }. TypeScript then knows it is a string inside the if.

exercises.prompt: What does the question mark mean in phone?: string?
choices: The property may be missing, so its type is string or undefined
The phone number must be checked by a regex
The value is private and hidden from logs
The field is computed by the database
exercises.explain: Optional properties force you to handle the missing case, for example with ?. and ??.

exercises.prompt: Data comes from an external API. Which type should you give it before checking it?
exercises.explain: unknown forces a check before use. any would let a wrong field name or a missing value go through unnoticed.

exercises.prompt: What is the return type of first(["seo", "ads"])?
exercises.explain: The generic T is inferred as string from the array, so the function returns a string.

exercises.prompt: With "strict": true in tsconfig.json, assigning null to a variable typed string is an error.
exercises.explain: True. strictNullChecks is part of strict mode: null and undefined must be declared explicitly, which removes a huge class of bugs.

exercises.prompt: What does this code print once compiled and run?
exercises.explain: typeof narrows the union: numbers go through toFixed(1), strings through toUpperCase. Both branches type-check.

exercises.prompt: What did TypeScript 7 change in July 2026?
choices: A compiler rewritten in Go, about ten times faster
A new syntax that replaces JavaScript
Types now checked by browsers at runtime
The end of support for interfaces
exercises.explain: Same language, much faster tooling. Large projects gain the most.

exercises.prompt: One line is rejected by the TypeScript compiler. Which one?
lines: interface Lead { email: string; score: number }
exercises.explain: email is a string; assigning a number to it is a type error, even though JavaScript would allow it.

exercises.prompt: Build the type of a status that can only be "new", "won" or "lost".
exercises.explain: A union of string literals: any other value is rejected at compile time.
